fixes.explanation: I understand the thought, because a lot of broken places get fixed up eventually. But look at the words. God says, "I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities will not be inhabited." Perpetual means no timer on it. Nothing in that verse says it's only for a while.

Right, nothing in this verse says it's only for a while. God says, "I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities will not be inhabited." Perpetual doesn't come with a reopening date. And the verse ends the same way as before: "Then you will know that I am the LORD."

That's right. God says the mountains will bear fruit for His people, "…for they will soon come home." Soon, friend. That comes in verse 8, right after the promise of fruit. After all that talk of ruins, it's a good word to hear.

Right, baker. People say the land devours men, but God says, "…you will no longer devour men or deprive your nation of its children, declares the Lord GOD." No longer. He's speaking to the land there, and what people say doesn't get the last word.

I see why you'd go there, because a mountain with open space sounds like a housing plan. But God says He will make Seir a desolate waste. He even says He will "…cut off from it those who come and go." (Ezekiel 35:7) That doesn't read like a place being set up for exiles to move into.

That's right. God says Seir "…delivered the Israelites over to the sword in the time of their disaster…" I think this one is heavy, and I'm not going to joke about it. It matters that God names what was done to His people.

That's the opposite of what God says. Seir did not hate bloodshed, so God says bloodshed will pursue it. Pursue is the word in that line, not spare. I think it's a heavy verse, so we'll stick to what it says.

That would be good news for Seir, and that's not what God says. He says that since Seir did not hate bloodshed, "…it will pursue you." Pursue means it keeps coming. Leave isn't the word in that verse, and it's a serious one.
That's the problem, baker. God says Seir made its claim "even though the LORD was there…" Seir said those lands would be its own, and the LORD was there. Bold doesn't even cover it.
That's it. God says, "You boasted against Me with your mouth and multiplied your words against Me. I heard it Myself!" Seir's words were about Israel's mountains, but God says they were aimed at Him.

Ezekiel, the prophet God is speaking through, is only the messenger here. God doesn't say Seir boasted against him. He says, "You boasted against Me with your mouth…" Ezekiel's just carrying the mail.

Yes, rejoices. God says, "While the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate." That's the timing He gives: the earth rejoices, and He makes Seir desolate. That's all the verse says about it, so I won't guess beyond it.

That's right. God says, "You will become a desolation, O Mount Seir, and so will all of Edom." Edom is another name for Esau, who settled in the hill country of Seir (Genesis 36:8). So the word reaches past one mountain to all of Edom.

The text actually widens it. God says, "You will become a desolation, O Mount Seir, and so will all of Edom." Edom is another name for Esau, who settled in the hill country of Seir (Genesis 36:8). So this reaches past one mountain to all of Edom.
That's right. God says, "…they have made you desolate and have trampled you on every side…" Every side, baker. He sees the whole picture of what Israel's mountains went through.

The text says it plainly. God says, "…they have made you desolate and have trampled you on every side…" So Israel's mountains were trampled all the way around. It's the opening of what God has to say to them.

Mountains growing taller would be quite a sight, but God doesn't say that. He says they "…will produce branches and bear fruit for My people Israel…" It's about what grows on them, not how tall they get. And the fruit is for His people.

That's it. God says, "…I am on your side; I will turn toward you, and you will be tilled and sown." Tilled means someone's working the ground again, and sown means seed is going in. And it all starts with God turning toward the mountains.
Buried isn't the word God uses. He promises, "The cities will be inhabited and the ruins rebuilt." Rebuilt is the word, and that's the promise for the ruins.

I see why that might sound right, since people were saying it. But God says to the land, "…you will no longer devour men or deprive your nation of its children, declares the Lord GOD." So He says the land will not keep on doing it. Read it again, and the answer turns around.
